entries.156962e3037592ca22579d13e114a3373720c6ea: <div sID="gen516" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="14" osisID="Gen.14" sID="Gen.14"/> <div eID="gen516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen517" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen518" type="x-p"/> We have four things in the story of this chapter. I. A war with the king of Sodom and his allies, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.1-Gen.14.11">ver. 1-11</reference>. II. The captivity of Lot in that war, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.12">ver. 12</reference>. III. Abram's rescue of Lot from that captivity, with the victory he obtained over the conquerors, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.13-Gen.14.16">ver. 13-16</reference>. IV. Abram's return from the expedition, (<reference osisRef="Gen.14.17">ver. 17</reference>), with an account of what passed, 1. Between him and the king of Salem, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.18-Gen.14.20">ver. 18-20</reference>. 2. Between him and the king of Sodom, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.21-Gen.14.24">ver. 21-24</reference>. So that here we have that promise to Abram in part fulfilled, that God would make his name great.
entries.908e7efa9acef144b5fb214ad3ef0d2071f47569: <div eID="gen518" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen517" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Lot Taken Captive. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1913.)</title> <div sID="gen519" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And it came to pass in the days of Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of nations; <hi type="super">2</hi> <hi type="italic">That these</hi> made war with Bera king of Sodom, and with Birsha king of Gomorrah, Shinab king of Admah, and Shemeber king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela, which is Zoar. <hi type="super">3</hi> All these were joined together in the vale of Siddim, which is the salt sea. <hi type="super">4</hi> Twelve years they served Chedorlaomer, and in the thirteenth year they rebelled. <hi type="super">5</hi> And in the fourteenth year came Chedorlaomer, and the kings that <hi type="italic">were</hi> with him, and smote the Rephaims in Ashteroth Karnaim, and the Zuzims in Ham, and the Emims in Shaveh Kiriathaim, <hi type="super">6</hi> And the Horites in their mount Seir, unto El-paran, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> by the wilderness. <hi type="super">7</hi> And they returned, and came to En-mishpat, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> Kadesh, and smote all the country of the Amalekites, and also the Amorites, that dwelt in Hazezontamar. 8 And there went out the king of Sodom, and the king of Gomorrah, and the king of Admah, and the king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela (the same <hi type="italic">is</hi> Zoar;) and they joined battle with them in the vale of Siddim; <hi type="super">9</hi> With Chedorlaomer the king of Elam, and with Tidal king of nations, and Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Ellasar; four kings with five. <hi type="super">10</hi> And the vale of Siddim <hi type="italic">was full of</hi> slimepits; and the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, and fell there; and they that remained fled to the mountain. <hi type="super">11</hi> And they took all the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah, and all their victuals, and went their way. <hi type="super">12</hi> And they took Lot, Abram's brother's son, who dwelt in Sodom, and his goods, and departed. <div eID="gen519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen520" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of the first war that ever we read of in scripture, which (though the wars of the nations make the greatest figure in history) we should not have had the history of if Abram and Lot had not been concerned in it. Now, concerning this war, we may observe, <div eID="gen520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen521" type="x-p"/> I. The parties engaged in it. The invaders were four kings, two of them no less than kings of Shinar and Elam (that is, Chaldea and Persia), yet probably not the sovereign princes of those great kingdoms in their own persons, but either officers under them, or rather the heads and leaders of some colonies which came out of those great nations, and settled themselves near Sodom, but retained the names of the countries from which they had their origin. The invaded were the kings of five cities that lay near together in the plain of Jordan, namely, Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim, and Zoar. Four of them are named, but not the fifth, the king of Zoar or Bela, either because he was much more mean and inconsiderable or because he was much more wicked and inglorious than the rest, and worthy to be forgotten. <div eID="gen521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen522" type="x-p"/> II. The occasion of this war was the revolt of the five kings from under the government of Chedorlaomer. Twelve years they served him. Small joy they had of their fruitful land, while thus they were tributaries to a foreign power, and could not call what they had their own. Rich countries are a desirable prey, and idle luxurious countries are an easy prey, to growing greatness. The Sodomites were the posterity of Canaan whom Noah had pronounced a servant to Shem, from whom Elam descended; thus soon did that prophecy begin to be fulfilled. In the thirteenth year, beginning to be weary of their subjection, they rebelled, denied their tribute, and attempted to shake off the yoke and retrieve their ancient liberties. In the fourteenth year, after some pause and preparation, Chedorlaomer, in conjunction with his allies, set himself to chastise and reduce the rebels, and, since he could not have it otherwise, to fetch his tribute from them on the point of his sword. Note, Pride, covetousness, and ambition, are the lusts from which wars and fightings come. To these insatiable idols the blood of thousands has been sacrificed. <div eID="gen522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen523" type="x-p"/> III. The progress and success of the war. The four kings laid the neighbouring countries waste and enriched themselves with the spoil of them (<reference osisRef="Gen.14.5-Gen.14.7">v. 5-7</reference>), upon the alarm of which it had been the wisdom of the king of Sodom to submit, and desire conditions of peace; for how could he grapple with an enemy thus flushed with victory? But he would rather venture the utmost extremity than yield, and it sped accordingly. <hi type="italic">Quos Deus destruet eos dementat—Those whom God means to destroy he delivers up to infatuation.</hi> 1. The forces of the king of Sodom and his allies were routed; and, it should seem, many of them perished in the slime-pits who had escaped the sword, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.10">v. 10</reference>. In all places we are surrounded with deaths of various kinds, especially in the field of battle. 2. The cities were plundered, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.11">v. 11</reference>. All the goods of Sodom, and particularly their stores and provisions of victuals, were carried off by the conquerors. Note, When men abuse the gifts of a bountiful providence to gluttony and excess, it is just with God, and his usual way, by some judgment or other to strip them of that which they have so abused, <reference osisRef="Hos.2.8-Hos.2.9">Hos. ii. 8, 9</reference>. 3. Lot was carried captive, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.12">v. 12</reference>. They took Lot among the rest, and his goods. Now Lot may here be considered, (1.) As sharing with his neighbours in this common calamity. Though he was himself a righteous man, and (which is here expressly noticed) Abram's brother's son, yet he was involved with the rest in all this trouble. Note, <hi type="italic">All things come alike to all,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.2">Eccl. ix. 2</reference>. The best of men cannot promise themselves an exemption from the greatest troubles in this life; neither from our own piety nor our relation to those that are the favourites of heaven will be our security, when God's judgments are abroad. Note, further, Many an honest man fares the worse for his wicked neighbours. It is therefore our wisdom to separate ourselves, or at least to distinguish ourselves, from them (<reference osisRef="2Cor.6.17">2 Cor. vi. 17</reference>), and so deliver ourselves, <reference osisRef="Rev.18.4">Rev. xviii. 4</reference>. (2.) As smarting for the foolish choice he made of a settlement here. This is plainly intimated when it is said, <hi type="italic">They took Abram's brother's son, who dwelt in Sodom.</hi> So near a relation of Abram should have been a companion and disciple of Abram, and should have abode by his tents; but, if he choose to dwell in Sodom, he must thank himself if he share in Sodom's calamities. Note, When we go out of the way of our duty we put ourselves from under God's protection, and cannot expect that the choices which are made by our lusts should issue to our comfort. Particular mention is made of their taking Lot's <hi type="italic">goods,</hi> those goods which had occasioned his contest with Abram and his separation from him. Note, It is just with God to deprive us of those enjoyments by which we have suffered ourselves to be deprived of our enjoyment of him.
entries.c72047ab3414ff64d47f6d44d38a5f9f6d7da1bd: <div eID="gen523" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Lot Taken Captive, and Rescued. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1913.)</title> <div sID="gen524" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> And there came one that had escaped, and told Abram the Hebrew; for he dwelt in the plain of Mamre the Amorite, brother of Eshcol, and brother of Aner: and these <hi type="italic">were</hi> confederate with Abram. <hi type="super">14</hi> And when Abram heard that his brother was taken captive, he armed his trained <hi type="italic">servants,</hi> born in his own house, three hundred and eighteen, and pursued <hi type="italic">them</hi> unto <reference osisRef="Dan.15">Dan. 15</reference> And he divided himself against them, he and his servants, by night, and smote them, and pursued them unto Hobah, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> on the left hand of Damascus. 16 And he brought back all the goods, and also brought again his brother Lot, and his goods, and the women also, and the people. <div eID="gen524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen525" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of the only military action we ever find Abram engaged in, and this he was prompted to, not by his avarice or ambition, but purely by a principle of charity; it was not to enrich himself, but to help his friend. Never was any military expedition undertaken, prosecuted, and finished, more honourably than this of Abram's. Here we have, <div eID="gen525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen526" type="x-p"/> I. The tidings brought him of his kinsman's distress. Providence so ordered it that he now sojourned not far off, that he might be a very present help. 1. He is here called <hi type="italic">Abram the Hebrew,</hi> that is, the son and follower of Heber, in whose family the profession of the true religion was kept up in that degenerate age. Abram herein acted like a Hebrew—in a manner not unworthy of the name and character of a religious professor. 2. The tidings were brought by one that had escaped with his life for a prey. Probably he was a Sodomite, and as bad as the worst of them; yet knowing Abram's relation to Lot, and concern for him, he implores his help, and hopes to speed for Lot's sake. Note, The worst of men, in the day of their trouble, will be glad to claim acquaintance with those that are wise and good, and so get an interest in them. The rich man in hell called Abram <hi type="italic">Father;</hi> and the foolish virgins made court to the wise for a share of their oil. <div eID="gen526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen527" type="x-p"/> II. The preparations he made for this expedition. The cause was plainly good, his call to engage in it was clear, and therefore, with all speed, he <hi type="italic">armed his trained servants, born in his house,</hi> to the number of <hi type="italic">three hundred and eighteen</hi>—a great family, but a small army, about as many as Gideon's that routed the Midianites, <reference osisRef="Judg.7.7">Judg. vii. 7</reference>. He drew out his <hi type="italic">trained</hi> servants, or his <hi type="italic">catechised</hi> servants, not only instructed in the art of war, which was then far short of the perfection which later and worse ages have improved it to, but instructed in the principles of religion; for Abram commanded his household to keep the way of the Lord. This shows that Abram was, 1. A great man, who had so many servants depending upon him, and employed by him, which was not only his strength and honour, but gave him a great opportunity of doing good, which is all that is truly valuable and desirable in great places and great estates. 2. A good man, who not only served God himself, but instructed all about him in the service of God. Note, Those that have great families have not only many bodies, but many souls besides their own, to take care of and provide for. Those that would be found the followers of Abram must see that their servants be catechised servants. 3. A wise man for, though he was a man of peace, yet he disciplined his servants for war, not knowing what occasion he might have, some time or other, so to employ them. Note, Though our holy religion teaches us to be for peace, yet it does not forbid us to provide for war. <div eID="gen527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen528" type="x-p"/> III. His allies and confederates in this expedition. He prevailed with his neighbours, <hi type="italic">Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre</hi> (with whom he kept up a fair correspondence) to go along with him. It was his prudence thus to strengthen his own troops with their auxiliary forces; and probably they saw themselves concerned, in interest, to act, as they could, against this formidable power, lest their own turn should be next. Note, 1. It is our wisdom and duty to behave ourselves so respectfully and obligingly towards all men as that, whenever there is occasion, they may be willing and ready to do us a kindness. 2. Those who depend on God's help, yet, in times of distress, ought to make use of men's help, as Providence offers it; else they tempt God. <div eID="gen528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen529" type="x-p"/> IV. His courage and conduct were very remarkable. 1. There was a great deal of bravery in the enterprise itself, considering the disadvantages he lay under. What could one family of husbandmen and shepherds do against the armies of four princes, who now came fresh from blood and victory? It was not a vanquished, but a victorious army, that he was to pursue; nor was he constrained by necessity to this daring attempt, but moved to it by generosity; so that, all things considered, it was, for aught I know, as great an instance of true courage as ever Alexander or Caesar was celebrated for. Note, Religion tends to make men, not cowardly, but truly valiant. The righteous is bold as a lion. The true Christian is the true hero. 2. There was a great deal of policy in the management of it. Abram was no stranger to the stratagems of war: He <hi type="italic">divided himself,</hi> as Gideon did his little army (<reference osisRef="Judg.7.16">Judg. vii. 16</reference>), that he might come upon the enemy from several quarters at once, and so make his few seem a great many; he made his attack by night, that he might surprise them. Note, Honest policy is a good friend both to our safety and to our usefulness. The serpent's head (provided it be nothing akin to the old serpent) may well become a good Christian's body, especially if it have a dove's eye in it, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.16">Matt. x. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen530" type="x-p"/> V. His success was very considerable, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.15-Gen.14.16">v. 15, 16</reference>. He defeated his enemies, and rescued his friends; and we do not find that he sustained any loss. Note, Those that venture in a good cause, with a good heart, are under the special protection of a good God, and have reason to hope for a good issue. Again, It is all one with the Lord <hi type="italic">to save by many or by few,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.6">1 Sam. xiv. 6</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen531" type="x-p"/> 1. He rescued his kinsman; twice here he is called his <hi type="italic">brother Lot.</hi> The remembrance of the relation that was between them, both by nature and grace, made him forget the little quarrel that had been between them, in which Lot had by no means acted well towards Abram. Justly might Abram have upbraided Lot with his folly in quarrelling with him and removing from him, and have told him that he was well enough served, he might have known when he was well off; but, in the charitable breast of pious Abram, it is all forgiven and forgotten, and he takes this opportunity to give a real proof of the sincerity of his reconciliation. Note, (1.) We ought to be ready, whenever it is in the power of our hands, to succour and relieve those that are in distress, especially our relations and friends. <hi type="italic">A brother is born for adversity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.17.17">Prov. xvii. 17</reference>. A friend in need is a friend indeed. (2.) Though others have been wanting in their duty to us, yet we must not therefore deny our duty to them. Some have said that they can more easily forgive their enemies than their friends; but we shall see ourselves obliged to forgive both if we consider, not only that our God, when we were enemies, reconciled us, but also that he <hi type="italic">passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.7.18">Mic. vii. 18</reference>. <div eID="gen531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen532" type="x-p"/> 2. He rescued the rest of the captives, for Lot's sake, though they were strangers to him and such as he was under no obligation to at all; nay, though they were Sodomites, sinners before the Lord exceedingly, and though, probably, he might have recovered Lot alone by ransom, yet he brought back all the women, and the people, and their goods, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.16">v. 16</reference>. Note, As we have opportunity we must do good to all men. Our charity must be extensive, as opportunity offers itself. Wherever God gives life, we must not grudge the help we can give to support it. God does good to the just and unjust, and so must we, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.45">Matt. v. 45</reference>. This victory which Abram obtained over the kings the prophet seems to refer to, <reference osisRef="Isa.41.2">Isa. xli. 2</reference>, <hi type="italic">Who raised up the righteous man from the east, and made him rule over kings?</hi> And some suggest that, as before he had a title to this land by grant, so now by conquest.
entries.26cf8328a56afa5f539689d1e5fd5335283bf8a8: <div eID="gen532" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Abram's Interview with Melchizedek. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1913.)</title> <div sID="gen533" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> And the king of Sodom went out to meet him after his return from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer, and of the kings that <hi type="italic">were</hi> with him, at the valley of Shaveh, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> the king's dale. <hi type="super">18</hi> And Melchizedek king of Salem brought forth bread and wine: and he <hi type="italic">was</hi> the priest of the most high God. <hi type="super">19</hi> And he blessed him, and said, Blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> Abram of the most high God, possessor of heaven and earth: <hi type="super">20</hi> And blessed be the most high God, which hath delivered thine enemies into thy hand. And he gave him tithes of all. <div eID="gen533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen534" type="x-p"/> This paragraph begins with the mention of the respect which the king of Sodom paid to Abram at his return from the slaughter of the kings; but, before a particular account is given of this, the story of Melchizedek is briefly related, concerning whom observe, <div eID="gen534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen535" type="x-p"/> I. Who he was. He was <hi type="italic">king of Salem</hi> and <hi type="italic">priest of the most high God;</hi> and other glorious things are said of him, <reference osisRef="Heb.7.1-Heb.7.10">Heb. vii. 1</reference>, &c. 1. The rabbin, and most of our rabbinical writers, conclude that Melchizedek was Shem the son of Noah, who was king and priest to those that descended from him, according to the patriarchal model. But this is not at all probable; for why should his name be changed? And how came he to settle in Canaan? 2. Many Christian writers have thought that this was an appearance of the Son of God himself, our Lord Jesus, known to Abram, at this time, by this name, as, afterwards, Hagar called him by another name, <reference osisRef="Gen.16.13">ch. xvi. 13</reference>. He appeared to him as a righteous king, owning a righteous cause, and giving peace. It is difficult to imagine that any mere man should be said to <hi type="italic">be without father, without mother, and without descent, having neither beginning of days nor end of life,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.7.3">Heb. vii. 3</reference>. It is witnessed of Melchizedek that he liveth, and that he abideth a priest continually (<reference osisRef="Heb.7.3">v. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.7.8">8</reference>); nay (<reference osisRef="Heb.7.13-Heb.7.14">v. 13, 14</reference>), the apostle makes him of whom these things are spoken to be our Lord who sprang out of Judah. It is likewise difficult to think that any mere man should, at this time, be greater than Abram in the things of God, that Christ should be a priest after the order of any mere man, and that any human priesthood should so far excel that of Aaron as it is certain that Melchizedek's did. 3. The most commonly received opinion is that Melchizedek was a Canaanitish prince, that reigned in Salem, and kept up the true religion there; but, if so, why his name should occur here only in all the story of Abram, and why Abram should have altars of his own and not attend the altars of his neighbour Melchizedek who was greater than he, seem unaccountable. Mr. Gregory of Oxford tells us that the <hi type="italic">Arabic Catena,</hi> which he builds much upon the authority of, gives this account of Melchizedek, That he was the son of Heraclim, the son of Peleg, the son of Eber, and that his mother's name was Salathiel, the daughter of Gomer, the son of Japheth, the son of Noah. <div eID="gen535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen536" type="x-p"/> II. What he did. 1. He <hi type="italic">brought forth bread and wine,</hi> for the refreshment of Abram and his soldiers, and in congratulation of their victory. This he did as a king, teaching us to do good and to communicate, and to be given to hospitality, according to our ability; and representing the spiritual provisions of strength and comfort which Christ has laid up for us in the covenant of grace for our refreshment, when we are wearied with our spiritual conflicts. 2. As priest of the most high God, he blessed Abram, which we may suppose a greater refreshment to Abram than his bread and wine were. Thus God, having raised up his Son Jesus, has sent him to bless us, as one having authority; and those whom he blesses are blessed indeed. Christ went to heaven when he was blessing his disciples (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.51">Luke xxiv. 51</reference>); for this is what he ever lives to do. <div eID="gen536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen537" type="x-p"/> III. What he said, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.19-Gen.14.20">v. 19, 20</reference>. Two things were said by him:—1. He blessed Abram from God: <hi type="italic">Blessed be Abram, blessed of the most high God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.14.19">v. 19</reference>. Observe the titles he here gives to God, which are very glorious. (1.) <hi type="italic">The most high God,</hi> which bespeaks his absolute perfections in himself and his sovereign dominion over all the creatures; he is King of kings. Note, It will greatly help both our faith and our reverence in prayer to eye God as the most high God, and to call him so. (2.) <hi type="italic">Possessor of heaven and earth,</hi> that is, rightful owner, and sovereign Lord, of all the creatures, because he made them. This bespeaks him a great God, and greatly to be praised (<reference osisRef="Ps.24.1">Ps. xxiv. 1</reference>), and those a happy people who have an interest in his favour and love. 2. He blessed God for Abram (<reference osisRef="Gen.14.20">v. 20</reference>): and <hi type="italic">blessed be the most high God.</hi> Note, (1.) In all our prayers, we must praise God, and join hallelujahs with all our hosannahs. These are the spiritual sacrifices we must offer up daily, and upon particular occasions. (2.) God, as the most high God, must have the glory of all our victories, <reference osisRef="Exod.17.15 1Sam.7.10 1Sam.7.12 Judg.5.1-Judg.5.2 2Chr.20.21">Exod. xvii. 15; 1 Sam. vii. 10, 12; Judg. v. 1, 2; 2 Chron. xx. 21</reference>. In them he shows himself higher than our enemies (<reference osisRef="Exod.18.11">Exod. xviii. 11</reference>), and higher than we; for without him we could do nothing. (3.) We ought to give thanks for others' mercies as for our own, triumphing with those that triumph. (4.) Jesus Christ, our great high priest, is the Mediator both of our prayers and praises, and not only offers up ours, but his own for us. See <reference osisRef="Luke.10.21">Luke x. 21</reference>. <div eID="gen537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen538" type="x-p"/> IV. What was done to him: <hi type="italic">Abram gave him tithes of all,</hi> that is, of the spoils, <reference osisRef="Heb.7.4">Heb. vii. 4</reference>. This may be looked upon, 1. As a gratuity presented to Melchizedek, by way of return for his tokens of respect. Note, Those that receive kindness should show kindness. Gratitude is one of nature's laws. 2. As an offering vowed and dedicated to the most high God, and therefore put into the hands of Melchizedek his priest. Note, (1.) When we have received some signal mercy from God, it is very fit that we should express our thankfulness by some special act of pious charity. God must always have his dues out of our substance, especially when, by any particular providence, he has either preserved or increased it to us. (2.) That the tenth of our increase is a very fit proportion to be set apart for the honour of God and the service of his sanctuary. (3.) That Jesus Christ, our great Melchizedek, is to have homage done him, and to be humbly acknowledged by every one of us as our king and priest; and not only the tithe of all, but all we have, must be surrendered and given up to him.
entries.340fb6a3cc8e469440811d8f45f78b7fda6e7c24: <div eID="gen538" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Abram's Disinterestedness. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1913.)</title> <div sID="gen539" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> And the king of Sodom said unto Abram, Give me the persons, and take the goods to thyself. <hi type="super">22</hi> And Abram said to the king of Sodom, I have lift up mine hand unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , the most high God, the possessor of heaven and earth, <hi type="super">23</hi> That I will not <hi type="italic">take</hi> from a thread even to a shoelatchet, and that I will not take any thing that <hi type="italic">is</hi> thine, lest thou shouldest say, I have made Abram rich: <hi type="super">24</hi> Save only that which the young men have eaten, and the portion of the men which went with me, Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre; let them take their portion. <div eID="gen539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen540" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of what passed between Abram and the king of Sodom, who succeeded him that fell in the battle (<reference osisRef="Gen.14.10">v. 10</reference>), and thought himself obliged to do this honour to Abram, in return for the good services he had done him. Here is, <div eID="gen540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen541" type="x-p"/> I. The king of Sodom's grateful offer to Abram (<reference osisRef="Gen.14.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">Give me the soul, and take thou the substance;</hi> so the Hebrew reads it. Here he fairly begs the persons, but as freely bestows the goods on Abram. Note, 1. Where a right is dubious and divided, it is wisdom to compound the matter by mutual concessions rather than to contend. The king of Sodom had an original right both to the persons and to the goods, and it would bear a debate whether Abram's acquired right by rescue would supersede his title and extinguish it; but, to prevent all quarrels, the king of Sodom makes this fair proposal. 2. Gratitude teaches us to recompense to the utmost of our power those that have undergone fatigues, run hazards, and been at expense for our service and benefit. <hi type="italic">Who goes a warfare at his own charges?</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.7">1 Cor. ix. 7</reference>. Soldiers purchase their pay dearer than any labourers, and are well worthy of it, because they expose their lives. <div eID="gen541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen542" type="x-p"/> II. Abram's generous refusal of this offer. He not only resigned the persons to him, who, being delivered out of the hand of their enemies, ought to have served Abram, but he restored all the goods too. He would not take <hi type="italic">from a thread to a shoe-latchet,</hi> not the least thing that had ever belonged to the king of Sodom or any of his. Note, A lively faith enables a man to look upon the wealth of this world with a holy contempt, <reference osisRef="1John.5.4">1 John v. 4</reference>. What are all the ornaments and delights of sense to one that has God and heaven ever in his eye? He resolves even to a thread and a shoe-latchet; for a tender conscience fears offending in a small matter. Now, <div eID="gen542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen543" type="x-p"/> 1. Abram ratifies this resolution with a solemn oath: <hi type="italic">I have lifted up my hand to the Lord that I will not take any thing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.14.22">v. 22</reference>. Here observe, (1.) The titles he gives to God, <hi type="italic">The most high God, the possessor of heaven and earth,</hi> the same that Melchizedek had just now used, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.19">v. 19</reference>. Note, It is good to learn of others how to order our speech concerning God, and to imitate those who speak well in divine things. This improvement we are to make of the conversation of devout good men, we must learn to speak after them. (2.) The ceremony used in this oath: <hi type="italic">I have lifted up my hand.</hi> In religious swearing we appeal to God's knowledge of our truth and sincerity and imprecate his wrath if we swear falsely, and the <hi type="italic">lifting up of the hand</hi> is very significant and expressive of both. (3.) The matter of the oath, namely, that he would not take any reward from the king of Sodom, was lawful, but what he was not antecedently obliged to. [1.] Probably Abram vowed, before he went to the battle, that, if God would give him success, he would, for the glory of God and the credit of his profession, so far deny himself and his own right as to take nothing of the spoils to himself. Note, the vows we have made when we are in pursuit of a mercy must be carefully and conscientiously kept when we have obtained the mercy, though they were made against our interest. A citizen of Zion, if he has sworn, whether it be to God or man, though it prove to <hi type="italic">his own hurt, yet he changeth not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.15.4">Ps. xv. 4</reference>. Or, [2.] Perhaps Abram, now when he saw cause to refuse the offer made him, at the same time confirmed his refusal with this oath, to prevent further importunity. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> There may be good reason sometimes why we should debar ourselves of that which is our undoubted right, as St. Paul, <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.13">1 Cor. viii. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.12">ix. 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That strong resolutions are of good use to put by the force of temptations. <div eID="gen543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen544" type="x-p"/> 2. He backs his refusal with a good reason: <hi type="italic">Lest thou shouldest say, I have made Abram rich,</hi> which would reflect reproach, (1.) Upon the promise and covenant of God, as if they would not have enriched Abram without the spoils of Sodom. And, (2.) Upon the piety and charity of Abram, as if all he had in his eye, when he undertook that hazardous expedition, was to enrich himself. Note, [1.] We must be very careful that we give no occasion to others to say things which they ought not. [2.] The people of God must, for their credit's sake, take heed of doing any thing that looks mean or mercenary, or that savours of covetousness and self-seeking. Probably Abram knew the king of Sodom to be a proud and scornful man, and one that would be apt to turn such a thing as this to his reproach afterwards, though most unreasonably. When we have to do with such men, we have need to act with particular caution. <div eID="gen544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen545" type="x-p"/> 3. He limits his refusal with a double proviso, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.24">v. 24</reference>. In making vows, we ought carefully to insert the necessary exceptions, that we may not afterwards say before the angel, <hi type="italic">It was an error,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.6">Eccl. v. 6</reference>. Abram here excepts, (1.) The food of his soldiers; they were worthy of their meat while they trod out the corn. This would give no colour to the king of Sodom to say that he had enriched Abram. (2.) The shares of his allies and confederates: <hi type="italic">Let them take their portion.</hi> Note, Those who are strict in restraining their own liberty yet ought not to impose those restraints upon the liberties of others, nor to judge of them accordingly. We must not make ourselves the standard to measure others by. A good man will deny himself that liberty which he will not deny another, contrary to the practice of the Pharisees, <reference osisRef="Matt.23.4">Matt. xxiii. 4</reference>. There was not the same reason why Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre, should quit their right, that there was why Abram should. They did not make the profession that he made, nor were they, as he was, under the obligation of a vow. They had not the hopes that Abram had of a portion in the other world, and therefore, by all means, <hi type="italic">let them take their portion</hi> of this.  <chapter eID="Gen.14"/> <div eID="gen545" type="x-p"/>

entries.80d0b9540eaa2e1e7e483d595f9cc00ce03f8f65: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv160"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 14</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Gen.14.1-Gen.14.24">Ge 14:1-24</reference>. War.</title> <div sID="gen317" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv160"/><hi type="bold">1. And it came to pass--</hi>This chapter presents Abram in the unexpected character of a warrior. The occasion was this: The king of Sodom and the kings of the adjoining cities, after having been tributaries for twelve years to the king of Elam, combined to throw off his yoke. To chastise their rebellion, as he deemed it, Chedorlaomer, with the aid of three allies, invaded the territories of the refractory princes, defeated them in a pitched battle where the nature of the ground favored his army (<reference osisRef="Gen.14.10">Ge 14:10</reference>), and hastened in triumph on his homeward march, with a large amount of captives and booty, though merely a stranger. <div eID="gen317" type="x-p"/>
entries.d65c9b5d75f9e85f61724c6af7c85b5058e663c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv161"/><div sID="gen318" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv161"/><hi type="bold">12. they took Lot ... and his goods, and departed--</hi>How would the conscience of that young man now upbraid him for his selfish folly and ingratitude in withdrawing from his kind and pious relative! Whenever we go out of the path of duty, we put ourselves away from God's protection, and cannot expect that the choice we make will be for our lasting good. <div eID="gen318" type="x-p"/>
entries.d0e743d94c59722dae036bb98e54f1df39aa2db4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv162"/><div sID="gen319" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv162"/><hi type="bold">13. there came one that had escaped--</hi>Abram might have excused himself from taking any active concern in his "brother," that is, nephew, who little deserved that he should incur trouble or danger on his account. But Abram, far from rendering evil for evil, resolved to take immediate measures for the rescue of Lot. <div eID="gen319" type="x-p"/>
entries.78668924fd5843c122698b803ee911dedfa889e4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv163"/><div sID="gen320" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv163"/><hi type="bold">14. And when Abram heard that his brother was taken captive, he armed his trained servants--</hi>domestic slaves, such as are common in Eastern countries still and are considered and treated as members of the family. If Abram could spare three hundred and eighteen slaves and leave a sufficient number to take care of the flocks, what a large establishment he must have had. <div eID="gen320" type="x-p"/>
entries.a720f7756a5a033b9641ef2bb18a89c68c27c7cc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv164"/><div sID="gen321" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv164"/><hi type="bold">15-16. he divided himself ... by night--</hi>This war between the petty princes of ancient Canaan is exactly the same as the frays and skirmishes between Arab chiefs in the present day. When a defeated party resolves to pursue the enemy, they wait till they are fast asleep; then, as they have no idea of posting sentinels, they rush upon them from different directions, strike down the tent poles--if there is any fight at all, it is the fray of a tumultuous mob--a panic commonly ensues, and the whole contest is ended with little or no loss on either side. <div eID="gen321" type="x-p"/>
entries.fe914756e0a8b8aa073f3c04a709c2bbc7796c3d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv165"/><div sID="gen322" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv165"/><hi type="bold">18. Melchizedek--</hi>This victory conferred a public benefit on that part of the country; and Abram, on his return, was treated with high respect and consideration, particularly by the king of Sodom and Melchizedek, who seems to have been one of the few native princes, if not the only one, who knew and worshipped, "the most high God," whom Abram served. This king who was a type of the Saviour (<reference osisRef="Heb.7.1">He 7:1</reference>), came to bless God for the victory which had been won, and in the name of God to bless Abram, by whose arms it had been achieved--a pious acknowledgment which we should imitate on succeeding in any lawful enterprise. <div eID="gen322" type="x-p"/>
entries.3f22e26733af8ed3bb8dfd692e872b184cebceff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv166"/><div sID="gen323" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv166"/><hi type="bold">20. he gave him tithes of all--</hi>Here is an evidence of Abram's piety, as well as of his valor; for it was to a priest or official mediator between God and him that Abram gave a tenth of the spoil--a token of his gratitude and in honor of a divine ordinance (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.9">Pr 3:9</reference>). <div eID="gen323" type="x-p"/>
entries.37780b08131f1cba2103c1bbe8dcc79695b19a9c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv167"/><div sID="gen324" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv167"/><hi type="bold">21. the king of Sodom said ... Give me the persons--</hi>According to the war customs still existing among the Arab tribes, Abram might have retained the recovered goods, and his right was acknowledged by the king of Sodom. But with honest pride, and a generosity unknown in that part of the world, he replied with strong phraseology common to the East, "I have lifted up mine hand" [that is, I have sworn] unto the Lord that I will not take from a thread even to a sandal-thong, and that that I will not take any thing that [is] thine, lest thou shouldst say, I have made Abram rich" [Ge 14:22, 23]. <chapter eID="Gen.14"/>

entries.89bfa4263c3b752abdcfdf0e2e95866e39bed8a3: <div eID="gen662" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen663" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen664" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen664" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen663" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen665" type="x-p"/> The war of four confederate kings against the five kings of Canaan, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.1-Gen.14.3">Gen 14:1-3</reference>. The confederate kings overrun and pillage the whole country, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.4-Gen.14.7">Gen 14:4-7</reference>. Battle between them and the kings of Canaan, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.5">Gen 14:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.9">Gen 14:9</reference>. The latter are defeated, and the principal part of the armies of the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah slain, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.10">Gen 14:10</reference>; on which these two cities are plundered, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.11">Gen 14:11</reference>. Lot, his goods, and his family, are also taken and carried away, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.12">Gen 14:12</reference>. Abram, being informed of the disaster of his nephew, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.13">Gen 14:13</reference>, arms three hundred and eighteen of his servants, and pursues them, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.14">Gen 14:14</reference>; overtakes and routs them, and recovers Lot and his family, and their goods, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.15">Gen 14:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.16">Gen 14:16</reference>; is met on his return by the king of Sodom, and by Melchizedek, king of Salem, with refreshments for himself and men, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.17">Gen 14:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.18">Gen 14:18</reference>. Melchizedek blesses Abram, and receives from him, as priest of the most high God, the tenth of all the spoils, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.19">Gen 14:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.20">Gen 14:20</reference>. The king of Sodom offers to Abram all the goods he has taken from the enemy, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.21">Gen 14:21</reference>; which Abram positively refuses, having vowed to God to receive no recompense for a victory of which he knew God to be the sole author, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.22">Gen 14:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.23">Gen 14:23</reference>; but desires that a proportion of the spoils be given to Aner, Eshcol and Mamre, who had accompanied him on this expedition, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.24">Gen 14:24</reference>. <div eID="gen665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen666" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen667" type="x-p"/> In the days of Amraphel - Who this king was is not known; and yet, from the manner in which he is spoken of in the text, it would seem that he was a person well known, even when Moses wrote this account. But the Vulgate gives a different turn to the place, by rendering the passage thus: Factum est in illo tempore, ut Amraphel, etc. "It came to pass in that time that Amraphel, etc." The Chaldee Targum of Onkelos makes Amraphel king of Babylon, others make him king of Assyria; some make him the same as Nimrod, and others, one of his descendants. <div eID="gen667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen668" type="x-p"/> Arioch king of Ellasar - Some think Syria is meant; but conjecture is endless where facts cannot be ascertained. Chedorlaomer king of Elam - Dr. Shuckford thinks that this was the same as Ninyas, the son of Ninus and Semiramis; and some think him to be the same with Keeumras, son of Doolaved, son of Arphaxad, son of Shem, son of Noah; and that Elam means Persia; see <reference osisRef="Gen.10.22">Gen 10:22</reference>. The Persian historians unanimously allow that Keeumras, whose name bears some affinity to Chedorlaomer, was the first king of the Peeshdadian dynasty. <div eID="gen668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen669" type="x-p"/> Tidal king of nations - גוים goyim, different peoples or clans. Probably some adventurous person, whose subjects were composed of refugees from different countries.
entries.b89c626d6648e9604fa731c2ee4ba6763a870e70: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen670" type="x-p"/> These made war with Bera, etc. - It appears, from <reference osisRef="Gen.14.4">Gen 14:4</reference>, that these five Canaanitish kings had been subdued by Chedorlaomer, and were obliged to pay him tribute; and that, having been enslaved by him twelve years, wishing to recover their liberty, they revolted in the thirteenth; in consequence of which Chedorlaomer, the following year, summoned to his assistance three of his vassals, invaded Canaan, fought with and discomfited the kings of the Pentapolis or five cities - Sodom, Gomorrah, Zeboiim, Zoar, and Admab, which were situated in the fruitful plain of Siddim, having previously overrun the whole land.
entries.9ba5868c41236b878b96adc673294290b9f2c453: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen671" type="x-p"/> Rephaims - A people of Canaan: <reference osisRef="Gen.15.20">Gen 15:20</reference>. <div eID="gen671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen672" type="x-p"/> Ashteroth - A city of Basan, where Og afterwards reigned; <reference osisRef="Jos.13.31">Jos 13:31</reference>. <div eID="gen672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen673" type="x-p"/> Zuzims - Nowhere else spoken of, unless they were the same with the Zamzummims, <reference osisRef="Deu.2.20">Deu 2:20</reference>, as some imagine. <div eID="gen673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen674" type="x-p"/> Emims - A people great and many in the days of Moses, and tall as the Anakim. They dwelt among the Moabites, by whom they were reputed giants; <reference osisRef="Deu.2.10">Deu 2:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.2.11">Deu 2:11</reference>. <div eID="gen674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen675" type="x-p"/> Shaveh Kiriathaim - Rather, as the margin, the plain of Kiriathaim, which was a city afterwards belonging to Sihon king of Heshbon; <reference osisRef="Jos.13.19">Jos 13:19</reference>.
entries.0c19a1ed0009dea4bce0e277ef4ab7ccbd6d85d2: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen676" type="x-p"/> The Horites - A people that dwelt in Mount Seir, till Esau and his sons drove them thence; <reference osisRef="Deu.2.22">Deu 2:22</reference>. <div eID="gen676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen677" type="x-p"/> El-paran - The plain or oak of Paran, which was a city in the wilderness of Paran; <reference osisRef="Gen.21.21">Gen 21:21</reference>.
entries.344a957b66f09f3411b0b38499e2a2d6ea5a21a8: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen678" type="x-p"/> En-mishpat - The well of judgment; probably so called from the judgment pronounced by God on Moses and Aaron for their rebellion at that place; <reference osisRef="Num.20.1-Num.20.10">Num 20:1-10</reference>. <div eID="gen678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen679" type="x-p"/> Amalekites - So called afterwards, from Amalek, son of Esau; <reference osisRef="Gen.36.12">Gen 36:12</reference>. <div eID="gen679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen680" type="x-p"/> Hazezon-tamar - Called, in the Chaldee, Engaddi; a city in the land of Canaan, which fell to the lot of Judah; <reference osisRef="Jos.15.62">Jos 15:62</reference>. See also <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.2">2Chr 20:2</reference>. It appears, from <reference osisRef="Sol.1.14">Sol 1:14</reference>, to have been a very fruitful place.
entries.4eb32e0385e87ce2d21325bdba5a1f90563bb067: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen681" type="x-p"/> Bela, the same is Zoar - That is, it was called Zoar after the destruction of Sodom, etc., mentioned in Genesis 19.
entries.cbc057fe03ad825eab486a449f353ec0c897e1ba: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen682" type="x-p"/> Slime-pits - Places where asphaltus or bitumen sprang out of the ground; this substance abounded in that country. <div eID="gen682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen683" type="x-p"/> Fell there - It either signifies they were defeated on this spot, and many of them slain, or that multitudes of them had perished in the bitumen-pits which abounded there; that the place was full of pits we learn from the Hebrew, which reads here בארת בארת beeroth beeroth, pits, pits, i.e., multitudes of pits. A bad place to maintain a fight on, or to be obliged to run through in order to escape.
entries.fcc004df9b8150d2db583759c069ae1d4a722cdf: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen684" type="x-p"/> They took all the goods, etc. - This was a predatory war, such as the Arabs carry on to the present day; they pillage a city, town, or caravan; and then escape with the booty to the wilderness, where it would ever be unsafe, and often impossible, to pursue them.
entries.8484d2ce6d372feb6eff683b739df37ff3f725c8: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen685" type="x-p"/> They took Lot, etc. - The people, being exceedingly wicked, had provoked God to afflict them by means of those marauding kings; and Lot also suffered, being found in company with the workers of iniquity. Every child remembers the fable of the Geese and Cranes; the former, being found feeding where the latter were destroying the grain, were all taken in the same net. Let him that readeth understand.
entries.da2740b6cc91a30953025e4684870ddcc3d74aea: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen686" type="x-p"/> Abram the Hebrew - See note on <reference osisRef="Gen.10.21">Gen 10:21</reference>. It is very likely that Abram had this appellation from his coming from beyond the river Euphrates to enter Canaan; for העברי haibri, which we render the Hebrew, comes from עבר abar, to pass over, or come from beyond. It is supposed by many that he got this name from Eber or Heber, son of Salah; see <reference osisRef="Gen.11.15">Gen 11:15</reference>. But why he should get a name from Heber, rather than from his own father, or some other of his progenitors, no person has yet been able to discover. We may, therefore, safely conclude that he bears the appellation of Hebrew or Ibrite from the above circumstance, and not from one of his progenitors, of whom we know nothing but the name, and who preceded Abram not less than six generations; and during the whole of that time till the time marked here, none of his descendants were ever called Hebrews; this is a demonstration that Abram was not called the Hebrew from Heber; see <reference osisRef="Gen.11.15-Gen.11.27">Gen 11:15-27</reference>. <div eID="gen686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen687" type="x-p"/> These were confederate with Abram - It seems that a kind of convention was made between Abram and the three brothers, Mamre, Eshcol, and Aner, who were probably all chieftains in the vicinity of Abram's dwelling: all petty princes, similar to the nine kings before mentioned.
entries.6bd4c2e1604a8bc632bb1b91c9f15e24fbf76e6a: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen688" type="x-p"/> He armed his trained servants - These amounted to three hundred and eighteen in number: and how many were in the divisions of Mamre, Eshcol, and Aner, we know not; but they and their men certainly accompanied him in this expedition. See <reference osisRef="Gen.14.24">Gen 14:24</reference>.
entries.3d53769ce59a41740ffa4497df796f8018040ee7: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen689" type="x-p"/> And he divided himself against them - It required both considerable courage and address in Abram to lead him to attack the victorious armies of these four kings with so small a number of troops, and on this occasion both his skill and his courage are exercised. His affection for Lot appears to have been his chief motive; he cheerfully risks his life for that nephew who had lately chosen the best part of the land, and left his uncle to live as he might, on what he did not think worthy his own acceptance. But it is the property of a great and generous mind, not only to forgive, but to forget offenses; and at all times to repay evil with good.
entries.96dd6456e7720ed94faffc180f439fb17ba7800c: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen690" type="x-p"/> And he brought back - the women also - This is brought in by the sacred historian with peculiar interest and tenderness. All who read the account must be in pain for the fate of wives and daughters fallen into the hands of a ferocious, licentious, and victorious soldiery. Other spoils the routed confederates might have left behind; and yet on their swift asses, camels, and dromedaries, have carried off the female captives. However, Abram had disposed his attack so judiciously, and so promptly executed his measures, that not only all the baggage, but all the females also, were recovered.
entries.45f2431f0cb105457be49594dc9ee44a451ef6d5: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen691" type="x-p"/> The king of Sodom went out to meet him - This could not have been Bera, mentioned <reference osisRef="Gen.14.2">Gen 14:2</reference>, for it seems pretty evident, from <reference osisRef="Gen.14.10">Gen 14:10</reference>, that both he and Birsha, king of Gomorrah, were slain at the bitumen-pits in the vale of Siddim; but another person in the meantime might have succeeded to the government.
entries.b562d6bfce2875228546a7ff044ad2c8c9e8c42a: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen692" type="x-p"/> And Melchizedek, king of Salem - A thousand idle stories have been told about this man, and a thousand idle conjectures spent on the subject of his short history given here and in Heb. vii. At present it is only necessary to state that he appears to have been as real a personage as Bera, Birsha, or Shinab, though we have no more of his genealogy than we have of theirs. <div eID="gen692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen693" type="x-p"/> Brought forth bread and wine - Certainly to refresh Abram and his men, exhausted with the late battle and fatigues of the journey; not in the way of sacrifice, etc.; this is an idle conjecture. <div eID="gen693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen694" type="x-p"/> He was the priest of the most high God - He had preserved in his family and among his subjects the worship of the true God, and the primitive patriarchal institutions; by these the father of every family was both king and priest, so Melchizedek, being a worshipper of the true God, was priest among the people, as well as king over them. <div eID="gen694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen695" type="x-p"/> Melchizedek is called here king of Salem, and the most judicious interpreters allow that by Salem, Jerusalem is meant. That it bore this name anciently is evident from <reference osisRef="Psa.76.1">Psa 76:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.76.2">Psa 76:2</reference> : "In Judah is God known; his name is great in Israel. In Salem also is his tabernacle, and his dwelling place in Zion." From the use made of this part of the sacred history by David, <reference osisRef="Psa.110.4">Psa 110:4</reference>, and by St. Paul, <reference osisRef="Heb.7.1-Heb.7.10">Heb 7:1-10</reference>, we learn that there was something very mysterious, and at the same time typical, in the person, name, office, residence, and government of this Canaanitish prince. 1. In his person he was a representative and type of Christ; see the scriptures above referred to. 2. His name, מלכי צדק malki tsedek, signifies my righteous king, or king of righteousness. This name he probably had from the pure and righteous administration of his government; and this is one of the characters of our blessed Lord, a character which can be applied to him only, as he alone is essentially righteous, and the only Potentate; but a holy man, such as Melchizedek, might bear this name as his type or representative. 3. Office; he was a priest of the most high God. The word כהן cohen, which signifies both prince and priest, because the patriarchs sustained this double office, has both its root and proper signification in the Arabic; kahana signifies to approach, draw near, have intimate access to; and from hence to officiate as priest before God, and thus have intimate access to the Divine presence: and by means of the sacrifices which he offered he received counsel and information relative to what was yet to take place, and hence another acceptation of the word, to foretell, predict future events, unfold hidden things or mysteries; so the lips of the priests preserved knowledge, and they were often the interpreters of the will of God to the people. Thus we find that Melchizedek, being a priest of the most high God, represented Christ in his sacerdotal character, the word priest being understood as before explained. 4. His residence; he was king of Salem. שלם shalam signifies to make whole, complete, or perfect; and hence it means peace, which implies the making whole the breaches made in the political and domestic union of kingdoms, states, families, etc., making an end of discord, and establishing friendship. Christ is called the Prince of peace, because, by his incarnation, sacrifice, and mediation, he procures and establishes peace between God and man; heals the breaches and dissensions between heaven and earth, reconciling both; and produces glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace and good will among men. His residence is peace and quietness and assurance for ever, in every believing upright heart. He governs as the Prince and Priest of the most high God, ruling in righteousness, mighty to save; and he ever lives to make intercession for, and save to the uttermost all who come unto the Father by him. See the notes on Hebrews 7 (note).
entries.5fdd7f2ef01253d479211ce435de33d14f1519b4: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen696" type="x-p"/> And he blessed him - This was a part of the priest's office, to bless in the name of the Lord, for ever. See the form of this blessing, <reference osisRef="Num.6.23-Num.6.26">Num 6:23-26</reference>; and for the meaning of the word to bless, see <reference osisRef="Gen.2.3">Gen 2:3</reference> (note).
entries.53477533e2c6dd75309794ad8807e3f5d9790543: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen697" type="x-p"/> And he gave him tithes - A tenth part of all the spoils he had taken from the confederate kings. These Abram gave as a tribute to the most high God, who, being the possessor of heaven and earth, dispenses all spiritual and temporal favors, and demands the gratitude, and submissive, loving obedience, of all his subjects. Almost all nations of the earth have agreed in giving a tenth part of their property to be employed in religious uses. The tithes were afterwards granted to the Levites for the use of the sanctuary, and the maintenance of themselves and their families, as they had no other inheritance in Israel.
entries.4cb8dfcf5daeef479dc62382b91b071e6a3b6c82: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen698" type="x-p"/> I have lift up mine hand - The primitive mode of appealing to God, and calling him to witness a particular transaction; this no doubt generally obtained among the faithful till circumcision, the sign of the covenant, was established. After this, in swearing, the hand was often placed on the circumcised part; see <reference osisRef="Gen.24.2">Gen 24:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.9">Gen 24:9</reference>.
entries.825f73117cd25825609cab1f0278cc4bb8fe8fb4: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen699" type="x-p"/> From a thread even to a shoelatchet - This was certainly a proverbial mode of expression, the full meaning of which is perhaps not known. Among the rabbinical writers חוט chut, or חוטי chuti, signifies a fillet worn by young women to tie up their hair; taken in this sense it will give a good meaning here. As Abram had rescued both the men and women carried off by the confederate kings, and the king of Sodom had offered him all the goods, claiming only the persons, he answers by protesting against the accepting any of their property: "I have vowed unto the Lord, the proprietor of heaven and earth, that I will not receive the smallest portion of the property either of the women or men, from a girl's fillet to a man's shoe-tie."
entries.439a4847fc3c2d5d2d1e79c396674f2e7b5c1571: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen700" type="x-p"/> Save only that which the young men have eaten - His own servants had partaken of the victuals which the confederate kings had carried away; see <reference osisRef="Gen.14.11">Gen 14:11</reference>. This was unavoidable, and this is all he claims; but as he had no right to prescribe the same liberal conduct to his assistants, Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre, he left them to claim the share that by right of conquest belonged to them of the recaptured booty. Whether they were as generous as Abram we are not told. <div eID="gen700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen701" type="x-p"/> The great variety of striking incidents in this chapter the attentive reader has already carefully noted. To read and not understand is the property of the foolish and the inconsiderate. 1. We have already seen the danger to which Lot exposed himself in preferring a fertile region, though peopled with the workers of iniquity. His sorrows commence in the captivity of himself and family, and the loss of all his property, though by the good providence of God he and they were rescued. 2. Long observation has proved that the company a man keeps is not an indifferent thing; it will either be the means of his salvation or destruction. 3. A generous man cannot be contented with mere personal safety while others are in danger, nor with his own prosperity while others are in distress. Abram, hearing of the captivity of his nephew, determines to attempt his rescue; he puts himself at the head of his own servants, three hundred and eighteen in number, and the few assistants with which his neighbors, Mamre, Aner, and Eshcol, could furnish him; and, trusting in God and the goodness of his cause, marches off to attack four confederate kings! 4. Though it is not very likely that the armies of those petty kings could have amounted to many thousands, yet they were numerous enough to subdue almost the whole land of Canaan; and consequently, humanly speaking, Abram must know that by numbers he could not prevail, and that in this case particularly the battle was the Lord's. 5. While depending on the Divine blessing and succor he knew he must use the means he had in his power; he therefore divided his troops skilfully that he might attack the enemy at different points at the same time, and he chooses the night season to commence his attack, that the smallness of his force might not be discovered. God requires a man to use all the faculties he has given him in every lawful enterprise, and only in the conscientious use of them can he expect the Divine blessing; when this is done the event may be safely trusted in the hands of God. 6. Here is a war undertaken by Abram on motives the most honorable and conscientious; it was to repel aggression, and to rescue the innocent from the heaviest of sufferings and the worst of slavery, not for the purpose of plunder nor the extension of his territories; therefore he takes no spoils, and returns peaceably to his own possessions. How happy would the world be were every sovereign actuated by the same spirit! 7. We have already noticed the appearance, person, office, etc., of Melchizedek; and, without indulging in the wild theories of either ancient or modern visionaries, have considered him as the Scriptures do, a type of Christ. All that has been already spoken on this head may be recapitulated in a few words. 1. The Redeemer of the world is the King of righteousness; he creates it, maintains it, and rules by it. 2. His empire is the empire of peace; this he proclaims to them who are afar off, and to them that are nigh; to the Jew and to the Gentile. 3. He is Priest of the most high God, and has laid down his life for the sin of the world; and through this sacrifice the blessing of God is derived on them that believe. Reader, take him for thy King as well as thy Priest; he saves those only who submit to his authority and take his Spirit for the regulator of their heart, and his word for the director of their conduct. How many do we find, among those who would be sorry to be rated so low as to rank only with nominal Christians, talking of Christ as their Prophet, Priest, and King, who are not taught by his word and Spirit, who apply not for redemption in his blood, and who submit not to his authority! Reader, learn this deep and important truth: "Where I am there also shall my servant be; and he that serveth me, him shall my Father honor."  <chapter eID="Gen.14"/> <div eID="gen701" type="x-p"/>

entries.d9a7cbec20442e719c5971a3e7a4bf255aa9b6e3: <reference osisRef="Gen.14.1-Gen.14.2">Gen 14:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen212" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Gen.14.1-Gen.14.3">Gen 14:1-3</reference> the account is introduced by a list of the parties engaged in war. The kings named here are not mentioned again. On <hi type="italic">Shinar</hi>, see <reference osisRef="Gen.10.10">Gen 10:10</reference>; and on <hi type="italic">Elam</hi>, Gen 10:22. It cannot be determined with certainty where <hi type="italic">Ellasar</hi> was. <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> supposes it to be <hi type="italic">Artemita</hi>, which was also called Χαλάσαρ, in southern Assyria, to the north of Babylon. <hi type="italic">Goyim</hi> is not used here for nations generally, but is the name of one particular nation or country. In <hi type="italic">Delitzsch</hi>'s opinion it is an older name for Galilee, though probably with different boundaries (cf. <reference osisRef="Josh.12.23">Jos 12:23</reference>; Jdg 4:2; and <reference osisRef="Isa.9.1">Isa 9:1</reference>). - The verb עשׂוּ (<hi type="italic">made</hi>), in <reference osisRef="Gen.14.2">Gen 14:2</reference>, is governed by the kings mentioned in Gen 14:1. To <hi type="italic">Bela</hi>, whose king is not mentioned by name, the later name <hi type="italic">Zoar</hi> (vid., <reference osisRef="Gen.19.22">Gen 19:22</reference>) is added as being better known.
entries.b7d0668fb98cb09ed29caccad16237c3df3fdc60: <reference osisRef="Gen.14.3">Gen 14:3</reference> <div eID="gen212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen213" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">All these</hi> (five kings) <hi type="italic">allied themselves together,</hi> (and came with their forces) <hi type="italic">into the vale of Siddim</hi> (השׂדּים, prob. fields of plains), <hi type="italic">which is the Salt Sea;</hi>” that is to say, which was changed into the Salt Sea on the destruction of its cities (<reference osisRef="Gen.19.24-Gen.19.25">Gen 19:24-25</reference>). That there should be five kings in the five cities (πεντάπολις, Wis. 10:6) of this valley, was quite in harmony with the condition of Canaan, where even at a later period every city had its king.
entries.3be52e3b89b73544f23211de469481357e74b50b: <reference osisRef="Gen.14.4-Gen.14.6">Gen 14:4-6</reference> <div eID="gen213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen214" type="x-p"/> The occasion of the war was the revolt of the kings of the vale of Siddim from Chedorlaomer. They had been subject to him for twelve years, “<hi type="italic">and the thirteenth year they rebelled</hi>.” In the fourteenth year Chedorlaomer came with his allies to punish them for their rebellion, and attacked on his way several other cities to the east of the Arabah, as far as the Elanitic Gulf, no doubt because they also had withdrawn from his dominion. The army moved along the great military road from inner Asia, past Damascus, through Peraea, where they smote the Rephaims, Zuzims, Emims, and Horites. “<hi type="italic">The Rephaim in Ashteroth Karnaim:</hi>” all that is known with certainty of the Rephaim is, that they were a tribe of gigantic stature, and in the time of Abram had spread over the whole of Peraea, and held not only Bashan, but the country afterwards possessed by the Moabites; from which possessions they were subsequently expelled by the descendants of Lot and the Amorites, and so nearly exterminated, that Og, king of Bashan, is described as the remnant of the Rephaim (<reference osisRef="Deut.2.20">Deu 2:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.3.11">Deu 3:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.3.13">Deu 3:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.12.4">Jos 12:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.13.12">Jos 13:12</reference>). Beside this, there were Rephaim on this side of the Jordan among the Canaanitish tribes (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.20">Gen 15:20</reference>), some to the west of Jerusalem, in the valley which was called after them the valley of the Rephaim (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.8">Jos 15:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.18.16">Jos 18:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.18">2Sa 5:18</reference>, etc.), others on the mountains of Ephraim (<reference osisRef="Josh.17.15">Jos 17:15</reference>); while the last remains of them were also to be found among the Philistines (2Sa 21:16.; 1Ch 20:4.). The current explanation of the name, viz., “the long-stretched,” or giants (<hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>), does not prevent our regarding רפא as the personal name of their forefather, though no intimation is given of their origin. That they were not Canaanites may be inferred from the fact, that on the eastern side of the Jordan they were subjugated and exterminated by the Canaanitish branch of the Amorites. Notwithstanding this, they may have been descendants of Ham, though the fact that the Canaanites spoke a Semitic tongue rather favours the conclusion that the oldest population of Canaan, and therefore the Rephaim, were of Semitic descent. At any rate, the opinion of <hi type="italic">J. G. Müller</hi>, that they belonged to the aborigines, who were not related to Shem, Ham, and Japhet, is perfectly arbitrary. - <hi type="italic">Ashteroth Karnaim</hi>, or briefly <hi type="italic">Ashtaroth</hi>, the capital afterwards of Og of Bashan, was situated in Hauran; and ruins of it are said to be still seen in <hi type="italic">Tell Ashtereh</hi>, two hours and a half from <hi type="italic">Nowah</hi>, and one and three-quarters from the ancient <hi type="italic">Edrei</hi>, somewhere between Nowah and Mezareib (see <hi type="italic">Ritter, Erdkunde</hi>).<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">J. G. Wetztein</hi>, however, has lately denied the identity of Ashteroth Karnaim, which he interprets as meaning Ashtaroth near Karnaim, with Ashtaroth the capital of Og (see <hi type="italic">Reiseber</hi>. <hi type="italic">üb. Hauran</hi>, etc. 1860, p. 107). But he does so without sufficient reason. He disputes most strongly the fact that Ashtaroth was situated on the hill Ashtere, because the Arabs now in Hauran assured him, that the ruins of this Tell (or hill) suggested rather a monastery or watch-tower than a large city, and associates it with the <hi type="italic">Bostra</hi> of the Greeks and Romans, the modern <hi type="italic">Bozra</hi>, partly on account of the central situation of this town, and its consequent importance to Hauran and Peraea generally, and partly also on account of the similarity in the name, as <hi type="italic">Bostra</hi> is the latinized form of <hi type="italic">Beeshterah</hi>, which we find in <reference osisRef="Josh.21.27">Jos 21:27</reference> in the place of the Ashtaroth of <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.56">1Ch 6:56</reference>; and that form is composed of <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> <hi type="italic">Ashtaroth</hi>, to which there are as many analogies as there are instances of the omission of <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> before the names of towns, which is a sufficient explanation of Ashtaroth (cf. <hi type="italic">Ges. thes.</hi>, p. 175 and 193).</note> <div eID="gen214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen215" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">The Zuzims in Ham</hi>” were probably the people whom the Ammonites called <hi type="italic">Zam</hi> <hi type="italic">zummim</hi>, and who were also reckoned among the Rephaim (<reference osisRef="Deut.2.20">Deu 2:20</reference>). <hi type="italic">Ham</hi> was possibly the ancient name of <hi type="italic">Rabba</hi> of the Ammonites (<reference osisRef="Deut.3.11">Deu 3:11</reference>), the remains being still preserved in the ruins of <hi type="italic">Ammân</hi>. - “<hi type="italic">The Emim in the plain of Kiryathaim</hi>:” the אימים or אמים (i.e., fearful, terrible), were the earlier inhabitants of the country of the Moabites, who gave them the name; and, like the Anakim, they were also reckoned among the Rephaim (<reference osisRef="Deut.2.11">Deu 2:11</reference>). <hi type="italic">Kiryathaim</hi> is certainly not to be found where Eusebius and Jerome supposed, viz., in Καριάδα, <hi type="italic">Coraiatha</hi>, the modern <hi type="italic">Koerriath</hi> or <hi type="italic">Kereyat</hi>, ten miles to the west of Medabah; for this is not situated in the plain, and corresponds to <hi type="italic">Kerioth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.24">Jer 48:24</reference>), with which <hi type="italic">Eusebius</hi> and <hi type="italic">Jerome</hi> have confounded <hi type="italic">Kiryathaim</hi>. It is probably still to be seen in the ruins of <hi type="italic">el Teym </hi>or <hi type="italic">et Tueme</hi>, about a mile to the west of Medabah. “<hi type="italic">The</hi> <hi type="italic">Horites</hi> (from חרי, dwellers in caves), <hi type="italic">in the mountains of Seir,</hi>” were the earlier inhabitants of the land between the Dead Sea and the Elanitic Gulf, who were conquered and exterminated by the Edomites (Gen 36:20.). - “<hi type="italic">To El-paran, which is by the wilderness:</hi>” i.e., on the eastern side of the desert of Paran (see <reference osisRef="Gen.21.21">Gen 21:21</reference>), probably the same as <hi type="italic">Elath</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.2.8">Deu 2:8</reference>) or <hi type="italic">Eloth</hi> (1Ki 9:26), the important harbour of <hi type="italic">Aila</hi> on the northern extremity of the so-called Elanitic Gulf, near the modern fortress of <hi type="italic">Akaba</hi>, where extensive heaps of rubbish show the site of the former town, which received its name <hi type="italic">El</hi> or <hi type="italic">Elath</hi> (<hi type="italic">terebinth</hi>, or rather <hi type="italic">wood</hi>) probably from the palm-groves in the vicinity.
entries.dbb9032de219b3285cef323aee9c57d6e1a4f24f: <reference osisRef="Gen.14.7">Gen 14:7</reference> <div eID="gen215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen216" type="x-p"/> From <hi type="italic">Aila</hi> the conquerors turned round, and marched (not through the Arabah, but on the desert plateau which they ascended from Aila) to <hi type="italic">En-mishpat</hi> (<hi type="italic">well of judgment</hi>), the older name of <hi type="italic">Kadesh</hi>, the situation of which, indeed, cannot be proved with certainty, but which is most probably to be sought for in the neighbourhood of the spring <hi type="italic">Ain Kades</hi>, discovered by <hi type="italic">Rowland</hi>, to the south of <hi type="italic">Bir Seba</hi> and <hi type="italic">Khalasa</hi> (<hi type="italic">Elusa</hi>), twelve miles E.S.E. of <hi type="italic">Moyle</hi>, the halting-place for caravans, near Hagar’s well (<reference osisRef="Gen.16.14">Gen 16:14</reference>), on the heights of <hi type="italic">Jebel Halal</hi> (see <hi type="italic">Ritter, Erdkunde,</hi> and Num 13). “<hi type="italic">And they smote all the country of the Amalekites,</hi>” i.e., the country afterwards possessed by the Amalekites (vid., <reference osisRef="Gen.26.12">Gen 26:12</reference>),<note placement="foot">The circumstance that in the midst of a list of tribes who were defeated, we find not the tribe but only the <hi type="italic">fields</hi> (שׂדה) of the Amalekites mentioned, can only be explained on the supposition that the nation of the Amalekites was not then in existence, and the country was designated proleptically by the name of its future and well-known inhabitants (Hengstenberg, Diss. ii. p. 249, translation).</note> to the west of Edomitis on the southern border of the mountains of Judah (Num 13:29), “<hi type="italic">and also the Amorites, who dwelt in Hazazon-Thamar,</hi>” i.e., <hi type="italic">Engedi</hi>, on the western side of the Dead Sea (<reference osisRef="2Chr.20.2">2Ch 20:2</reference>).
entries.d6f83b5337a321ba7bb2ae37071fa5e42f0c4814: <reference osisRef="Gen.14.8-Gen.14.12">Gen 14:8-12</reference> <div eID="gen216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen217" type="x-p"/> After conquering all these tribes to the east and west of the Arabah, they gave battle to the kings of the Pentapolis in the vale of Siddim, and put them to flight. The kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fell there, the valley being full of asphalt-pits, and the ground therefore unfavourable for flight; but the others escaped to the mountains (הרה for ההרה), that is, to the Moabitish highlands with their numerous defiles. The conquerors thereupon plundered the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah, and carried off Lot, who dwelt in Sodom, and all his possessions, along with the rest of the captives, probably taking the route through the valley of the Jordan up to Damascus.
entries.9dfaca7a1dce6ccb50d146d32ccc3fc762680ecf: <reference osisRef="Gen.14.13-Gen.14.16">Gen 14:13-16</reference> <div eID="gen217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen218" type="x-p"/> A fugitive (lit., <hi type="italic">the</hi> fugitive; the article denotes the genus, <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §277) brought intelligence of this to Abram the <hi type="italic">Hebrew</hi> (העברי, an immigrant from beyond the Euphrates). Abram is so called in distinction from Mamre and his two brothers, who were Amorites, and had made a defensive treaty with him. To rescue Lot, Abram <hi type="italic">ordered his trained slaves </hi>(חניכיו, i.e., practised in arms) <hi type="italic">born in the house</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.17.12">Gen 17:12</reference>), 318 <hi type="italic">men, to turn out</hi> (lit., to pour themselves out); and with these, and (as the supplementary remark in <reference osisRef="Gen.14.24">Gen 14:24</reference> shows) with his allies, he pursued the enemy as far as <hi type="italic">Dan</hi>, where “<hi type="italic">he divided himself against them, he and his servants, by night,</hi>” - i.e., he divided his men into companies, who fell upon the enemy by night from different sides - “<hi type="italic">smote them, and pursued them to Hobah, to the left</hi> (or north) <hi type="italic">of Damascus</hi>.” Hobah has probably been preserved in the village of Noba, mentioned by <hi type="italic">Troilo</hi>, a quarter of a mile to the north of Damascus.
